topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: What is the purpose of the standardized signals described in the Guide's Water Skiing Signals diagram?
choice_a: To let the skier and the boat operator communicate instructions such as speed changes, turns, and stopping without relying on shouted words
choice_b: To notify nearby anglers that a diver is submerged in the area
choice_c: To indicate which docks are reserved for personal watercraft rental customers
choice_d: To mark the boundary of a no-wake zone near a boating access area
explanation: The Guide's Water Skiing section provides a standardized set of hand signals (Faster, Slower, Speed O.K., Right Turn, Left Turn, Back To Drop-Off Area, Cut Motor, Stop, Skier O.K. After Fall, and Pick Me Up/Fallen Skier--Watch Out) so the skier and boat operator can communicate clearly during towing.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing - Water Skiing Signals

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: Which of the following is one of the standardized hand signals listed in the Guide's Water Skiing Signals section?
explanation: "Cut Motor" is one of the ten standardized signals listed in the Guide's Water Skiing Signals diagram, alongside Faster, Slower, Speed O.K., Right Turn, Left Turn, Back To Drop-Off Area, Stop, Skier O.K. After Fall, and Pick Me Up/Fallen Skier--Watch Out.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing - Water Skiing Signals

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: Which of the following is one of the standardized hand signals listed in the Guide's Water Skiing Signals section, used to tell the boat operator where to return the skier?
explanation: "Back To Drop-Off Area" is one of the ten standardized signals listed in the Guide's Water Skiing Signals diagram.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing - Water Skiing Signals

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: Per the Guide, which single signal in the Water Skiing Signals list serves two different meanings depending on the situation?
explanation: The Guide lists "PICK ME UP or FALLEN SKIER--WATCH OUT" as a single combined signal covering both meanings, unlike the other nine signals in the diagram, which each carry only one meaning.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing - Water Skiing Signals

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A parent brings their 10-year-old child boating and allows the child to operate a personal watercraft while the parent rides along on the PWC the entire time. Under the Guide, is this lawful?
choice_a: No, because no person under 14 years of age may operate a PWC regardless of adult accompaniment
choice_b: Yes, because a person of any age may operate a PWC if accompanied by a parent or guardian
choice_c: Yes, as long as the child wears a Coast Guard approved PFD
choice_d: No, because the child must be at least 12 years old even with adult accompaniment
explanation: The exception allowing a 14- to 16-year-old to operate a PWC while accompanied by an adult who occupies the PWC applies only once the operator is at least 14. No person under 14 years of age may operate a PWC under any circumstance, including with an adult aboard.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Minimum Age To Operate

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC operator is traveling at 8 mph in the same direction as, and within 40 feet to the rear of, another underway vessel, outside of any narrow channel. Under the Guide's definition of "following too closely," has a violation occurred?
choice_a: No, because the violation requires exceeding 10 mph in addition to being within the specified distance
choice_b: Yes, because 40 feet is within the 100-foot rear distance threshold
choice_c: Yes, because any speed within 100 feet to the rear is a violation
choice_d: No, because the following-too-closely rule only applies to PWCs following other PWCs
explanation: "Following too closely" requires both proceeding at a speed in excess of 10 mph and approaching within 100 feet to the rear (or 50 feet to the side) of another underway vessel. At 8 mph, the speed element is not met even though the distance element is, so no violation occurs.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Reckless Operation (Following Too Closely)

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC is operating in a channel that is 250 feet wide, following 30 feet behind another vessel at 18 mph, matching the speed and flow of surrounding vessel traffic. Under the Guide, is this a "following too closely" violation?
choice_a: No, because the channel is 300 feet or less in width, so a PWC may operate at the speed and flow of other vessel traffic there
choice_b: Yes, because 18 mph exceeds the general 10 mph threshold regardless of channel width
choice_c: Yes, because 30 feet is closer than the 50-foot side distance threshold
choice_d: No, because the following-too-closely rule never applies inside any channel
explanation: A narrow channel is defined as a segment of State waters 300 feet or less in width. Within a narrow channel, the following-too-closely speed/distance rule does not apply, and a PWC may instead operate at the speed and flow of other vessel traffic.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Reckless Operation (Following Too Closely, narrow channel definition)

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC operator jumps the wake of another vessel that is 130 feet away, and visibility around that vessel is not obstructed. Does this act, standing alone, fall under the Guide's specifically listed reckless-operation example of "jumping the wake of another vessel"?
choice_a: No, because that listed example applies only within 100 feet of the other vessel, or when visibility around it is obstructed
choice_b: Yes, because jumping any wake is reckless regardless of distance under this specific example
choice_c: No, because wake-jumping is never covered anywhere in the reckless operation rule
choice_d: Yes, because 130 feet is within a 150-foot safety zone described in the Guide
explanation: The Guide's listed example of reckless PWC operation is jumping the wake of another vessel within 100 feet of that vessel, or when visibility around it is obstructed. At 130 feet with unobstructed visibility, neither condition of that specific example is met.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Reckless Operation

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC operator is traveling in a narrow channel and passes 70 feet from an anchored vessel without reducing to no-wake speed. Under the Guide, has a violation of the PWC no-wake-speed restriction occurred?
choice_a: No, because the no-wake requirement in a narrow channel only applies within 50 feet of the anchored vessel
choice_b: Yes, because 70 feet is within the standard 100-foot no-wake distance
choice_c: Yes, because no-wake speed is required at all times in a narrow channel
choice_d: No, because anchored vessels are not protected by the no-wake restriction
explanation: The 100-foot no-wake-speed restriction around anchored or moored vessels, docks, piers, swim areas, swimmers, and manually operated vessels is reduced to 50 feet when the PWC is operating in a narrow channel. At 70 feet in a narrow channel, no violation occurs.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Other Operating Restrictions

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A boat tows a water skier at 1:00 a.m. during an authorized regatta, without a rear vision mirror, an observer, or the skier wearing a life preserver. Under the Guide, is this lawful?
choice_a: Yes, because the nighttime-hours prohibition and the mirror/observer/life-preserver requirement do not apply to professional skiing exhibitions or authorized regattas
choice_b: No, because towing skiers at night is always prohibited with no exceptions
choice_c: No, because a life preserver on the skier is always mandatory even during authorized regattas
choice_d: Yes, because regattas are exempt from all water skiing regulations, including the reckless-manner prohibition
explanation: The Guide states that the prohibition on towing between one hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise, and the requirement for a mirror, observer, or life preserver at other times, do not apply to professional skiing exhibitions or authorized regattas.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: Sunset today is at 7:00 p.m. A boat tows a water skier at 7:20 p.m. without a rear vision mirror, without an observer aboard, and the skier is not wearing a life preserver. Under the Guide, is this lawful?
choice_a: No, because 7:20 p.m. is not yet within the absolute nighttime prohibition, but towing at any time other than the restricted hours still requires a mirror, an observer, or a life preserver, and none is present
choice_b: No, because towing skiers is prohibited at any time after sunset, with no exceptions
choice_c: Yes, because the nighttime prohibition does not begin until one hour after sunset, and no other requirement applies before then
choice_d: Yes, because the mirror/observer/life-preserver rule only applies during the day
explanation: The absolute towing prohibition runs from one hour after sunset (8:00 p.m. here) to one hour before sunrise. Before that window begins, towing is lawful only if the vessel has a rear vision mirror, or an observer aboard, or the skier wears a life preserver; at 7:20 p.m. none of those three conditions is met, so towing is unlawful even though the absolute nighttime ban has not yet started.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Water Skiing

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A vessel's only safe navigable route through a narrow waterway passes directly over a spot where a diver's flag is displayed, with no reasonable way to route around it. Must the vessel still stay at least 50 feet away from the flag?
choice_a: No, the 50-foot minimum approach distance does not apply where the flagged location would otherwise constitute an unreasonable obstruction to navigation
choice_b: Yes, the 50-foot distance applies in all circumstances with no exceptions
choice_c: No, the minimum approach distance rule applies only to PWCs, not other vessels
choice_d: Yes, but only during daylight hours; at night the distance requirement does not apply
explanation: The Guide provides that vessels may not approach closer than 50 feet to any structure displaying a diver's flag, except when it is located so as to constitute an unreasonable obstruction to navigation.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Skin and Scuba Divers

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC's manufacturer identifies its maximum safe load as 3 persons. The operator wants to have an observer aboard while towing 2 skiers at once, for a total of 4 people counted between the vessel and those being towed. Under the Guide, is this lawful?
choice_a: No, because the total number of persons operating, observing, and being towed may not exceed the manufacturer's maximum safe load of 3
choice_b: Yes, because towed skiers do not count toward the manufacturer's maximum safe load
choice_c: Yes, as long as each skier wears a Coast Guard approved PFD
choice_d: No, because PWCs may never tow more than one skier at a time regardless of rated capacity
explanation: The Guide requires that the total number of persons operating, observing, and being towed not exceed the number of passengers identified by the manufacturer as the vessel's maximum safe load; here 4 exceeds the rated capacity of 3.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Towing Skiers

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A PWC operator repeatedly swerves side to side on an otherwise empty stretch of water with no other vessels within several hundred yards. Does this conduct, standing alone, meet the Guide's specifically listed reckless-operation example of "weaving through congested vessel traffic"?
choice_a: No, because that listed example requires weaving through vessel traffic that is congested, which is not present here
choice_b: Yes, because any repeated swerving is automatically "weaving through congested traffic" under the Guide
choice_c: No, because weaving is never mentioned anywhere in the Guide's PWC rules
choice_d: Yes, because the Guide defines "congested" as any area with more than one vessel present all day
explanation: The Guide's listed example is "unreasonably or unnecessarily weaving through congested vessel traffic" - congestion is a required element of that specific example, though the same conduct could still be evaluated as reckless under the general reasonable-and-prudent-operation standard.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Personal Watercraft - Reckless Operation

topic: Operation of Vessels, PWC & Water Sports
question: A vessel in a channel that is 200 feet wide passes 80 feet from a law enforcement vessel displaying a flashing blue light, without reducing to no-wake speed. Under the Guide, has a violation occurred?
choice_a: No, because in a narrow channel the no-wake requirement applies only within 50 feet of the law enforcement vessel, and 80 feet is outside that distance
choice_b: Yes, because 80 feet is within the standard 100-foot threshold
choice_c: Yes, because any vessel in a channel must always operate at no-wake speed
choice_d: No, because the law enforcement no-wake rule applies only to PWCs
explanation: Vessels must slow to no-wake speed when passing within 100 feet of a law enforcement vessel displaying a flashing blue light, but only within 50 feet when in a narrow channel. At 80 feet in this 200-foot-wide (narrow) channel, no violation occurs.
source_note: NC Vessel Operator's Guide, Operation of Vessels - Law Enforcement Vessels
